 ORAL DECISION I am ready to render my decision in this appeal. The appellant, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, appeals the refusal to approve the sponsored application of his wife, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, the applicant. The applicant was refused, because she was found to be a member of an inadmissible class of persons described in section 19(1)(b) of the Immigration Act. Specifically, the visa officer found there were reasonable grounds to believe that the applicant would be unable or unwilling to support herself. The visa officer was not satisfied that adequate arrangements, other than those, which involve social assistance, had been made for her care and support. Material to the visa officer’s decision was at the time the appellant undertook to sponsor the applicant, he was in receipt of welfare. Also as indicated in the visa officer’s refusal letter found in the record, the visa officer was of the view that the applicant would not be able to support herself, noting that she had poor English skills. I am just going to cite a few facts that provide the background to this appeal. The appellant came to Canada in 1993 as a refugee. He made a refugee claim, which was accepted approximately six months later. He was initially on social assistance until approximately September 1994 when he became employed. He was laid off in December 1995. He then received unemployment insurance for approximately six months, after which time he enrolled at Seneca College as a full-time student. He received welfare benefits from June 1996 until February 1998 while he was attending school. He now has a diploma from Seneca College, and although he has been unable to obtain employment in his desired field, he has been continuously employed since February 1998. The evidence in support of this appeal is essentially found in the appellant’s testimony and the supporting documents found in Exhibit A-1. The overall credibility of this evidence was not 
1999 CanLII 14699 (CA IRB)
 T98-06416 
 2contested by the respondent. The appellant’s testimony was clear, forthright and uncontradicted. I, therefore, find his evidence in support of this appeal to be credible and trustworthy. This evidence establishes the following. The appellant received welfare benefits for approximately one and a half years in the past nearly five years. During that time, he was in full-time attendance at school, upgrading his employment skills. He has been employed continuously since February 1998. He currently holds two jobs and makes between $32,000 and $35,000 a year working approximately 60 hours a week. The appellant has made inquiries with his former supervisor at Axiom Plastics regarding the work prospects for the applicant and he has received positive indications that she will receive employment there. His current salary is sufficient to meet his living needs. According to the evidence, as calculated by the respondent, the appellant’s income, less his financial obligations, would leave approximately $350 a month disposable income should his wife be able to come to Canada. I note that part of his financial obligations are student loan payments. These amounts were not corroborated. However, the appellant’s estimation of approximately $400 to $500 a month, does not seem to be unreasonable, based as it is on his comparison with others similarly situated. The Minister’s representative contends that the $350 estimated disposable income is insufficient for the appellant and the applicant. The appellant maintains that it is sufficient, given that this money is to be used for non-essentials. I note that the appellant presented detailed evidence regarding his income and expenses. His work history indicates that he is a responsible individual. These observations considered in light of the other aforementioned evidence, lead me to find that the appellant is able to support the applicant and

 3that adequate arrangements other than those which involve social assistance, have been made for her care and support. I, therefore, conclude that the refusal is invalid in law and it is for these reasons that I allow this appeal. (Edited for grammar and syntax) ORDER The Immigration Appeal Division orders that the appeal be allowed
 because the refusal to approve the application for landing made by: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX is not in accordance with the law. “N. Kelley” N. XXXXXX DATED at Toronto this 8th 
 day of December , 1999. 
You have the right under ss. 82.1(1) of the Immigration Act to apply for a judicial review of this decision, with leave of a judge of the Federal Court - Trial Division. You may wish to consult with counsel immediately as your time for applying for leave is limited under that section.
